title: 3-Read Friday #127 Cognitive Hot Dogs, Curious Brains, and Atomising Fractions
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly 3-Read Friday curates three recent education blog posts and adds his own editorial framing for each. This issue pairs Benjamin Riley's argument that the brain-as-computer model is a warped mirror, so that AI works more like a tempting "cognitive hot dog" than a tutor, with Vicky Brooks on why clarity is the second step of a good explanation rather than the first. The third pick is Dylan Kane's practical atomisation of fraction addition, chosen because it suggested a different way to teach the procedure, with a shout-out to Julie's atomisations of subtraction and equations. Barton explains why each piece caught him, noting that Riley's piece is uncomfortable for someone who works with AI daily. The issue links learning-science ideas about prior mental models and working memory to concrete classroom choices.
points: Riley's argument that minds are feedback-control systems, not computers, reframes AI as something that can quietly undermine what schools exist to protect.
Brooks's point that students arrive with mental models that already feel complete means teachers must create wondering or prediction before explaining.
Kane's atomised fraction addition shows how sidestepping shaky multiplication frees working memory for the connections that hold a procedure together.
Barton's curation signals that practical atomisation examples across subtraction, equations and fractions are now an active thread among teacher bloggers.
quotes: Ben takes a break from his compelling Alpha School series to write a piece that's uncomfortable for anyone who spends much of their time working with AI (i.e., me). He argues that the brain-as-computer model is a warped mirror.

Our minds are feedback-control systems, shaped by millions of years of biological and cultural evolution. Seen that way, AI looks less like a tutor and more like a cognitive hot dog — tempting in the moment, but quietly undermining what schools exist to protect.
I am obsessed with teacher explanations. We all know that a good explanation needs to be clear and concise, but Vicky argues that clarity is the second step, not the first.
Students arrive with mental models that already feel complete. Unless they’re wondering, predicting or wrestling with something before we explain, even our best explanations can land flat.
This week, there have been some cracking posts on practical examples of atomisation. I chose Dylan’s because it got me thinking about a different way to teach adding fractions

In this piece, Dylan shows how sidestepping students’ shaky multiplication frees up working memory for the connections that hold a procedure together. And yes, he tackles the “won’t they lose the big picture?” objection head-on.
